title: Specs and captain cards read like a person wrote them
public_title: Write specs and captain cards for a human reader
acceptance: Governing rule. Any text that firstmate or a crew member writes for a person to read must be a shared language that both a human and an AI agent can read without decoding: specs, captain cards, pull-request titles and bodies, commit messages, and every comment or status that firstmate or crew posts to GitHub. The rules live in one file, skills/firstmate/plain-writing.md (Change 1). The target reader is a backend engineer with three to five years of experience who knows git and CI but has never seen this repository. Machine tokens that parsers need (a task number at the start of a title or commit subject, APPROVE:, REJECT:, ASK- and WORKER_ markers, fm-note markers, EVIDENCE: lines) stay exactly as they are, and each one is accompanied by plain text that says what it means.

Why. Our specs and captain cards read like compressed machine notes, so a person has to decode them before judging them. One real example, from the first acceptance line of the T-1003 spec: "Main87df introduced T269 contradiction checks using any(k in record for k in merge_keys) before nonmerge exclusion." Here a commit hash is glued to a word, a task number is used as if every reader knows it, and "nonmerge exclusion" names a code path the sentence never explains. The captain reads every card and approves every spec, so unreadable text turns an approval into a guess. Workers and reviewers then spend rounds on questions a clear spec would have answered. The STE checks in bin/lib/fm_ste.py keep sentences short and active, but they do not catch text that is short and still unreadable. Two MIT-licensed guides list the patterns that make text read like AI output: github.com/blader/humanizer (English) and github.com/kevintsai1202/Humanizer-zh-TW (Traditional Chinese). The captain decided on 2026-10-09: write specs and captain cards for a backend engineer with three to five years of experience who has never seen this repository; keep one reviewer, the spec preflight reviewer, and let it fix wording itself; check all three card languages; give every card a why, a how and a glossary; and let the final code reviewer write merge cards.

Change 1, the writing rules. Add skills/firstmate/plain-writing.md, the one place that defines how firstmate and reviewers write a spec or a captain card. It names the target reader: a backend engineer with three to five years of experience who knows git and CI but has never seen this repository. It lists the humanizer patterns adapted to our documents, with credit and the MIT notice for both sources. It adds our own rules: explain a term of art in one plain sentence the first time it appears; never make an internal code (a task number, a decision ID, a commit hash) the subject of a sentence, but say what the thing is and put the code in parentheses; keep a number apart from the word next to it; give each acceptance line one requirement. It states the order of priority from the humanizer guides: keep every fact, number, condition, scope and level of certainty first, and improve wording only after that. fm_plain.py implements three mechanical checks, after removing code spans in backquotes, URLs, repository paths (a token containing a slash and either a dot or a top-level repository directory name such as bin, board, tests, design, skills or i18n), hexadecimal hashes of seven or more characters, task numbers, decision IDs, version numbers such as 2.55 or v1.2, and machine markers: a glued number is a letter directly followed by a digit or a digit directly followed by a letter inside one word ("All13", "ts2672"); a slash chain is three or more words joined by slashes ("kindchoice/purposerepin/chosenA"); an unexplained term is a glossary term that matches in the text (Change 2 matching) while its id is not in the document's glossary list. Only cards have a glossary list that an author writes; a pull-request body gets its glossary section generated from the terms it uses (Change 14), so the unexplained-term check never blocks pull-request text. The checks block in three places: card requests (check-plain: all three checks), new pr-authoring drafts (fm_self_pr.py validate: glued number and slash chain) and spec preflight of public fields (Change 15: glued number and slash chain). Everywhere else, including commit messages and posted comments, they are advisory: they write findings to firstmate's log and never stop a commit or a post.

Change 2, the glossary file. Add i18n/glossary.json with this schema: {"schema": 1, "terms": [entry, ...]}. Each entry is {"id": string, "en": {"term": string, "aliases": [string, ...], "text": string}, "zh-TW": {same three keys}}. id matches ^[a-z][a-z0-9-]*$ and is unique. text is one plain sentence that passes the STE fact check of bin/lib/fm_ste.py. The first entries are pin, repin, standing-item, gate, six-gates, carry, door, spec-ok, preflight, round, brief, autopilot, board, scope and fail-first. plain-writing.md points to this file and does not copy it. zh-CN text comes from zh-TW through i18n/tw2cn.tsv, as for every other text. Change 2, glossary matching. bin/lib/fm_plain.py finds glossary terms in card text. In en it matches the term or an alias as a whole word, ignoring case. In zh-TW it matches the term or an alias as a substring. When two matches overlap, the longer one wins and the shorter one inside it is not a match. Every human-visible card field is searched: title, explanation, before, after, outcome, the option descriptions, pros and cons, the text of intent, why, how, done, notes and questions, scope_in and scope_out, change_points how, door reason and rollback, check q, why and options, before_nodes and after_nodes labels, and change_table text. Glossary explanations themselves are not searched, so an explanation never needs its own glossary entry. fm_plain.py refuses a glossary.json with a duplicate id, a missing locale, or an empty term or text.

Change 3, a standing workflow rule. skills/firstmate/SKILL.md states that firstmate writes every spec, captain card, pull-request text and commit message by plain-writing.md, as a rule of the workflow and not a habit of one session. skills/reviewer/SKILL.md states the reviewer duties in Changes 4 to 11 and the fenced blocks they use. skills/worker/SKILL.md states that worker notes posted to a pull request (.fm-say.md) follow plain-writing.md and keep their machine markers.

Change 4, readability in spec preflight. prompt() in bin/lib/fm_spec_preflight.py adds readability as one more standing category, read as the target reader from Change 1. prompt() loads skills/firstmate/plain-writing.md and i18n/glossary.json from the frozen code root and includes their text. If either file is missing, prompt() raises ValueError naming the file, and the launcher exits 65 before any model runs. fm_spec_preflight.py imports fm_plain.py and reads these files only inside prompt() and retain(), never at module import, so evidence readers that import fm_spec_preflight (bin/lib/fm_evidence.py) and the module list in tests/e2e/lib/fixture.ts need no new file.

Change 4, readability items. Each readability item quotes the exact sentence and says where the target reader gets stuck. A wording problem that the reviewer fixes in its rewrite is written `N. ok:` and says the rewrite fixes it. A problem that a clear rewrite cannot fix without changing meaning is written `N. gap:` with the expected spec change. Later passes keep the existing transitions from design section 6 (Spec preflight and migration): an earlier gap or open becomes done or open, an earlier ok or done becomes ok or open, and new findings are appended as `gap NEW-GROUND:` or `gap MISSED:`.

Change 5, where the rewrite goes. The reviewer may return the whole spec with improved wording in one fenced block whose opening line is exactly ```json fm-reworded-spec. The block goes before item 1 of the numbered checklist, never between the last item and PREFLIGHT-COMPLETE. The existing rule that only blank lines may separate the last item from PREFLIGHT-COMPLETE stays unchanged, in the prompt and in skills/reviewer/SKILL.md. _standing_block() and structure() already ignore fenced blocks; a regression test keeps that true for this block. Change 5, extracting rewrite blocks. A rewrite block is a line that is exactly ```json fm-reworded-spec, ```json fm-reworded-card or ```json fm-reworded-pr-authoring, followed by content, followed by a line that is exactly ```. For each kind: no block means no rewrite; exactly one block whose content is one JSON object is a candidate; a second block of the same kind is refused with reason duplicate; content that is not one JSON object is refused with reason not-an-object; a card or pr-authoring block in a run that did not receive that input is refused with reason unsolicited. A refused block makes the effective outcome rewrite-refused (Change 7). The retained answer text and the reviewer's verdict stay exactly as returned, and the existing rule that a checklist with a gap or open item must end in SPEC-GAPS still applies to the reviewer's answer. A block with no closing line hides the rest of the answer from the existing readers, so the final has no readable verdict: it is an invalid final, retain() stores no receipt, the outcome is failed, the command exits 65, and firstmate reruns the preflight. Nothing in a fenced block is ever read as a verdict.

Change 6, what a spec rewrite may change. Only title and the text of each acceptance line may change; every other key, including id, milestone, depends_on, scope, public_title, public_summary, public_changes, change_refs, check_answer, adopt and explain, must be identical after JSON parsing, and the acceptance list keeps its length and order. For each changed string separately, fm_plain.py compares the multiset of protected tokens and refuses the rewrite when they differ. Protected tokens are code spans in backquotes, repository paths, file:line references, hexadecimal hashes of seven or more characters, task numbers (T- followed by digits), decision IDs (D- followed by an identifier) and every number. This guard catches dropped, added or moved tokens but does not prove that meaning is unchanged; the prompt and skills/reviewer/SKILL.md require the reviewer to state in its checklist that each rewritten string keeps its meaning, and a rewrite that would change a condition or obligation is a gap, not a rewrite. A rewrite that passes the guard is revalidated with every check prompt() applies to a submitted spec, including validate_change_refs(), adopt validation, the explain STE check and, with FM_EXTERNAL=1, the external public-text check in bin/lib/fm_public_text.py; a failing rewrite is refused. The reviewer does not rewrite public_title, public_summary or public_changes, because a token guard cannot tell whether ordinary words came from private spec text; a readability problem in those fields is a gap that firstmate fixes, and the prompt tells the reviewer to check that public fields contain no private prose.

Change 7, the receipt keeps the reviewer's answer and adds an effective result. retain() keeps spec_sha256 as the SHA-256 of the submitted bytes and keeps verdict as the reviewer's own marker, so authenticated provenance and Store.records() checks are unchanged. It adds a rewrite object with, for the spec and for the card from Change 11, the rewritten SHA-256, status accepted or refused, and the refusal reason. When any rewrite is refused, the effective outcome is rewrite-refused. When a later preflight runs on the same task, prompt() adds the previous receipt's refusal reasons as a separate block after the verbatim standing list, without changing any retained text.

Change 7, which bytes a receipt authorizes. require_ok() authorizes bytes in two cases: the SHA-256 equals spec_sha256 of a SPEC-OK receipt that has no spec rewrite, or it equals an accepted spec rewrite SHA-256 of a SPEC-OK receipt. A receipt with a spec rewrite never authorizes the submitted bytes. A receipt whose effective outcome is rewrite-refused authorizes nothing. outcome() still looks receipts up by the submitted SHA-256 and returns rewrite-refused for such a receipt. The preflight command exits 65 for rewrite-refused, as it does for SPEC-GAPS. The existing rejection rules also apply to an accepted rewrite's bytes: bytes that any retained receipt marked SPEC-GAPS are never authorized, and retain() refuses SPEC-OK for unchanged bytes that were rejected before.

Change 7, handing over the bytes. The launcher bin/lib/fm-spec-preflight.sh writes an accepted spec rewrite to spec-preflight/out/spec.reworded.json in the run directory, byte for byte as retained, and prints one line: `fm-review: reworded spec <path> sha256 <sha>`. It does the same for an accepted card rewrite at spec-preflight/out/card.reworded.json. firstmate puts exactly those bytes in the task file and in the card request.

Change 8, why, how and glossary on every card. Card details gain, in both en and zh-TW, a how list with the same item shape as why ({kind, text}), and a glossary list of glossary ids. A new subcommand, fm_ste.py check-plain <file>, refuses details that lack a nonempty why, a nonempty how or a glossary list; refuses a glossary id that i18n/glossary.json does not have; refuses a matched term from Change 2 whose id is not listed; and reports STE results for every how item. _report() includes how items in the STE report for every card that has them. check-plain also checks the item shape ({kind, text}) of why and how and reports STE results for why and how on every card, with or without intent.

Change 8, why no longer forces an intent card. _validate() in fm_ste.py treats a card as an intent card only when it has intent or one of the other intent fields, not when it has only why, how or glossary. Today a card with why and no intent is refused, so this change only accepts cards that used to be refused.

Change 8, every card request is checked. bin/fm-decide.sh --request runs check-plain on every request with --details, for every kind (choice, merge and merge-untracked), before any file is written. fm-decide then expands each glossary id into {id, term, text} for that locale from i18n/glossary.json and stores the expanded list in the pending details, so the card keeps the explanation it had when it was raised. The legacy title-only path for D-SK requests (bin/fm-decide.sh, the branch after the details path) is an intentional compatibility exception: it stays accepted, unchanged, for callers outside this repository; no producer in this repository uses it after this task, and a regression test keeps it working. Change 8, the skill-update producer. bin/fm.sh self-update writes bilingual why (from --why), how (what adoption does) and glossary into the details it builds, so its card passes check-plain; tests/skill-update-cards.test.sh runs the real self-update command end to end and asserts the raised card carries all three in en and zh-TW. A newly raised card always expands ids from the current glossary.json; code that copies an existing card's glossary converts the stored objects back to their ids first.

Change 9, the card review is part of the same preflight. bin/fm-review.sh --spec-preflight accepts an optional --card <details.json> for a dispatch or repin card. The launcher copies the card into the run directory as read-only pinned bytes, like the spec, and records its SHA-256. The same run, with the same reader and rules, reviews the card text in en, zh-TW and zh-CN. fm_plain.py renders the zh-CN text for the prompt by applying the i18n/tw2cn.tsv rows in file order, exactly as board/server.ts sends them and board/public/index.html applies them; this task does not change that order. Change 9, zh-CN findings. A word left in Traditional characters in the rendered zh-CN text is a readability item. The reviewer either rewords zh-TW so that the table converts it, or lists the exact missing i18n/tw2cn.tsv rows in the item; adding rows to the table is ordinary repository work, not part of the rewrite.

Change 10, which card fields a card rewrite may change. The reviewer may return the improved card in one fenced block whose opening line is exactly ```json fm-reworded-card, placed before item 1, with the same malformed-block rules as Change 5. Only these prose strings may change, in each locale: title, explanation, before, after, outcome, options.X.description, pros and cons, and the text of why, how, notes and questions items, before_nodes and after_nodes labels, and change_table text. Everything else, including effect, purpose, kind, intent, done, scope_in, scope_out, change_points, door, check, glossary ids, item kinds and every list length, must be identical. The protected-token guard of Change 6 applies to each changed string, and check-plain must accept the result. Change 10, the card receipt is a record, not a gate. The receipt records the card's submitted SHA-256 and the accepted card rewrite SHA-256. fm-decide does not refuse a card for lacking a receipt in this task. skills/firstmate/SKILL.md requires firstmate to request a dispatch or repin card with the reviewed card bytes.

Change 11, the merge card block. An APPROVE final may include one fenced block whose opening line is exactly ```json fm-merge-card, holding title, why, how, notes and glossary in en and zh-TW, written by plain-writing.md and describing what the reviewed head actually changed. retain_verdict() in bin/lib/fm_evidence.py extracts it into a merge_card field of the verdict record and records merge_card_status: present, absent, malformed (more than one block, unclosed, or not one JSON object) or ignored (on a REJECT). The full answer text stays as today. verdict_marker() and criteria() already ignore fenced blocks; regression tests keep that true. The reviewer writes this in the same review call, not in an extra one.

Change 11, which review the merge card comes from. bin/lib/fm_autopilot_loop.py passes build() the readiness record it already holds. build() in bin/lib/fm_merge_details.py takes merge_card only from the verdict that readiness record selected: the verdict's signature must equal the readiness record's verdict_signature, the readiness record's task, project and pr must equal the card's task, project and PR number, and the readiness head must equal the gated head. A carried approval, where gate 6 accepted an unchanged patch on a new head, is valid in the same way it is valid for gate 6. The pinned spec text used for the path check is the text whose SHA-256 equals the selected verdict's binding spec_sha256, read the way source_binding() in bin/lib/fm_binding.py reads it, including its committed-spec fallback.

Change 11, building the merge card. With a usable merge_card, build() uses its why, how, notes and glossary, and uses its title as the text after the MERGE CARD prefix; it keeps intent, scope_in, scope_out, done, options and the fixed merge sentences as today, and requires every path and code span in the block to appear in the reviewed diff's file list or in the pinned spec text. Otherwise build() falls back to the current copy of the dispatch card, adds the caution note "Not reviewed for readability" in both locales, and copies why, how and glossary from the dispatch card when it has them, converting stored glossary objects back to ids. In both cases build() adds the ids of glossary terms that its own fixed sentences use, then runs check-plain on the fully composed card; any failure raises ValueError, and the autopilot's existing "merge card details needed" wake asks firstmate to author the details before any request. The timing does not change.

Change 11, privacy. The fm-merge-card block never leaves local evidence. bin/fm-review.sh removes fm-merge-card blocks from the verdict text it projects to a pull-request comment, and with FM_EXTERNAL=1 it keeps the block only in the private store. The captain's click on the board stays the only merge authorization. With FM_EXTERNAL=1 a test plants a private sentinel inside the block and shows that local evidence keeps it while every public projection (comment, summary and thread reply) excludes it, also for duplicate and unclosed blocks. A spec rewrite that changes public_title, public_summary or public_changes is refused (Change 6); a test plants a private prose sentinel with no path, ID, hash or number in a rewritten public_summary and shows the rewrite is refused and nothing reaches publication.

Change 12, the board. board/server.ts and board/public/index.html render why, how and the glossary on every card shape that has them: the main card, the detail sheet and the enriched (walk) card. why and how appear as two titled lists; the glossary appears as its own section below them, each entry showing term and text. A card without these fields renders exactly as today. board/public/board.css styles the sections. The labels use two new keys, card.how and card.glossary, in i18n/ui.en.json and i18n/ui.zh-TW.json, with zh-CN through i18n/tw2cn.tsv. The end-to-end test includes a non-intent card that carries why, how and glossary, compares the zh-CN card text with an independently written expectation, and uses a conversion table with overlapping rows to show the board and fm_plain.py convert the same way.

Change 14, self pull-request text. firstmate writes the prose fields of state/pr-authoring/<task>.json (subject, problem, expected_result, approach and the intent_notes notes) by plain-writing.md. The same spec-preflight run reviews them: bin/fm-review.sh --spec-preflight accepts an optional --pr-authoring <file>, pins it like the card, and the reviewer may return improved prose in one fenced block whose opening line is exactly ```json fm-reworded-pr-authoring, placed before item 1, under the malformed-block rules of Change 5. Only those prose fields may change; every other key and the intent_notes indexes stay identical, the protected-token guard of Change 6 applies to each changed string, the reviewer states in its checklist that each rewritten field keeps its meaning, and an accepted rewrite must pass fm_self_pr.py validate (subject verb, ASCII, length and index rules) or it is refused with the same effective outcome and exit code as a spec rewrite. When the same run also accepts a spec rewrite, the launcher sets the spec entry of the pr-authoring sources to the rewritten spec's SHA-256, records that this is the only machine change, and validates the result against the rewritten spec; the accepted pr-authoring SHA-256 and the exported bytes include this adjustment. When the spec rewrite is accepted and a pr-authoring input was supplied without a prose rewrite, the launcher still writes the adjusted draft (only the spec digest changed) as the accepted pr-authoring output. This is how a reviewed draft seals against the reviewed spec. The receipt records the submitted and accepted SHA-256 and the launcher writes accepted bytes to spec-preflight/out/pr-authoring.reworded.json with the same printed line. fm_self_pr.py validate keeps its current checks and adds the blocking mechanical checks of Change 1 (glued number and slash chain) on the prose fields. These prose checks run only when a draft is validated for sealing a new pull request; render() and preview() of an already sealed envelope keep only the structural and binding validation they have today, so old envelopes still render.

Change 14, the rendered pull-request body. render() in bin/lib/fm_self_pr.py starts the body with a Why section (problem) and a How section (approach), then the existing sections, and ends with a Glossary section listing every glossary term the title and body use, with its en explanation. The question-draft body gets the same Why section and glossary. The title keeps its form, task number, colon and subject, and the 85-character limit. bin/fm-worker.sh and bin/fm-canary.sh call render() and preview() unchanged. Tests cover the small, complex and question bodies, an old sealed envelope rendering and previewing unchanged except for the new sections, and a new draft with a glued number refused at sealing.

Change 15, external pull-request text. For an external project, the title and body come from the spec's public_title, public_summary and public_changes through bin/lib/fm_pr_format.py and the project's confirmed conventions. Those spec fields follow plain-writing.md; firstmate writes them and fixes any readability gap the reviewer reports, since the reviewer may not rewrite them (Change 6); and the blocking mechanical checks of Change 1 run on those fields only during spec preflight (on the submitted spec and on a rewrite), through a new function in bin/lib/fm_public_text.py. fm_public_text.validate() itself, which bin/fm-worker.sh and bin/lib/fm_pr_format.py call on every round, is unchanged, so an already approved pin whose public fields break the new checks still publishes on its next round; a test shows this with such a fixture. The project's own template, section names and title style (for example conventional commits) win wherever they conflict with plain-writing.md; plain-writing.md governs only the prose inside them.

Change 16, commit messages. Commits that firstmate's launcher writes keep the task number prefix that parsers read. The subject of the round commit (bin/fm-worker.sh, also used by the rebuild commit-tree) stays the spec title for the self project and the public title for an external project, so it follows the spec rules. The generic fallback subject "<task>: project work" becomes "<task>: Save the round's changes", mid-run checkpoints keep the worker's own message ("<task>: <message>", which the worker writes by its role skill), and only the stop and recovery checkpoint that bin/fm-worker.sh requests with a reason changes from "checkpoint (<reason>)" to "Save unfinished work after the round stopped (<reason>)". Every reader of these subjects is listed and keeps working: the PR-title adoption check in bin/fm-worker.sh that compares against "<task>: project work" also accepts the new fallback, and old commits and pull requests with the old text stay recognized. Tests cover a mid-run checkpoint, a stop checkpoint, the prefixed-message form, recognition of the old and the new fallback title, and the rebuild commit-tree subject.

Change 17, comments and statuses posted to GitHub. Fixed text that firstmate composes is rewritten by plain-writing.md and keeps its machine markers: the rebuild note in bin/fm-worker.sh (a short why and what-to-do, plus the existing head lines), the external projection summary and the status description in bin/lib/fm_external.py, and the reviewer comment projection wrapper in bin/fm-review.sh (the EVIDENCE line stays). Text that crew authors (worker notes, reviewer verdicts, external thread replies) follows the role skills from Change 3; before posting, bin/lib/fm_plain.py lint reports glued numbers, slash chains and unexplained glossary terms to firstmate's log without blocking the post. On the base, config.yaml selects comments for the self project and unnamed self callers default to comments (bin/fm-config.sh), so these paths apply to the self project too. Tests in tests/worker-notes.test.sh, tests/external-reviews.test.sh and tests/lib/plain_writing.py post a worker note, a reviewer comment and an external thread reply that break the advisory checks, and show that each post still happens, machine markers are unchanged, and the finding reaches firstmate's log. bin/fm-merge.sh passes no message of its own; GitHub's default merge text is the pull-request title, which Change 14 covers. firstmate creates no issues, and .github templates are filled by people, so neither is changed.

Change 18, the design. design/design.md section 6 (subsection Spec preflight and migration) describes the readability category, the three rewrite blocks, the guards, the receipt fields and the effective outcome. Section 5.2 (Captain decisions) describes how, glossary, check-plain and glossary expansion. Section 5.4 (The pull request protocol) describes pull-request text, commit messages and posted comments. Section 8 (The captain's board) describes the new card sections and the merge card source. Each edit stays inside its numbered section and adds nothing after the last numbered section. The preflight protocol keeps its rule of at least one checklist item per acceptance line.

Migration. Existing pins, preflight receipts, verdict records and pending or answered cards are not rewritten. A receipt without a rewrite object authorizes its exact submitted bytes as today. A verdict without merge_card_status reads as absent. Cards already raised render as today. A review final without an fm-merge-card block goes through the fallback in Change 11. Rounds already running finish on their frozen code. Isolated test copies that run prompt() or fm-decide copy plain-writing.md, glossary.json and fm_plain.py: tests/lib/review.sh and tests/lib/external_public_title.py are updated to do so. fm_ste.py imports fm_plain.py only inside check-plain, so modules that import fm_ste for other checks, and the module list in tests/e2e/lib/fixture.ts, need no new file. Existing pull requests, commits and comments are not edited. Old pr-authoring files without the new mechanical properties still render; validate refuses them only when they are next sealed for a new pull request. The fallback commit subject change is recognized in both directions by the adoption check. Fixtures: Fixtures. New-card request fixtures in tests/decide.test.sh, tests/board-card-effects.test.sh, tests/board-readiness.test.sh, tests/decisions.test.sh and tests/skill-update-cards.test.sh gain why, how and glossary and copy the new files they need. Separate historical-card fixtures keep their old shape and keep passing, to prove old records still read.

Tests. Behavioural fail-first tests drive entrypoints that exist on the current base, so on the base they fail at a named behavioural assertion, not at an import error or unknown flag: a spec rewrite through the existing --spec-preflight without new flags; card, merge, pr-authoring and commit behaviour through fm-decide.sh --request, fm_merge_details.build, fm_self_pr.py render and the worker launcher. Tests of new interfaces (--card, --pr-authoring, check-plain and fm_plain.py) are labelled interface tests; on the base they fail at argument parsing and are not counted as behavioural evidence. Cases: fm-decide.sh --request (refusing a card without how on choice, merge, merge-untracked and the deferred-validation path; glossary expansion; request, answer, fallback build and second request), the preflight launcher with a stub vendor final (rewrite blocks for spec, card and pr-authoring; malformed, duplicate and unclosed blocks; changed effect; changed public_summary; a number moved between two acceptance lines; a semantic gap marked by the reviewer next to a rewrite yielding SPEC-GAPS; rewrite-refused with exit 65; a fresh Store.records() read of an authenticated rewritten receipt; exported bytes equal to retained bytes and to the authorized hash; refusal reasons reaching the next prompt; a readability item open then done across two passes; input mutation during review not reaching the pinned copy; an unchanged card reviewed without rewrite), fm_merge_details.build (valid block; stale head, other task, project or PR, superseded review and carried approval; invented path; fallback missing why, how or glossary; composed fixed sentences gaining glossary ids), fm_self_pr.py render and validate (Why, How and Glossary sections; glued number refused), fm-worker.sh and fm-checkpoint.sh commit subjects, fm_external.py summary text, and the board end-to-end test tests/e2e/board-plain-card.spec.ts (main card, detail sheet and walk card in en, zh-TW and zh-CN, and an old card unchanged). tests/i18n.test.sh asserts card.how and card.glossary in both ui files with an explicit zh-CN expectation, the caution sentence's conversion, and STE on every glossary.json entry. Direct unit tests of fm_plain.py in tests/lib/plain_writing.py are extra and labelled as such. Named glossary cases: en whole-word match and a non-match inside a longer word, case-insensitive match, alias match, zh-TW substring match, the longer of two overlapping terms winning, a term only in a previously excluded field (intent, done, door, node label) now matched, and duplicate ids or a missing locale refused. Merge-block retention cases, each read back by a fresh Store: duplicate, unclosed, not-an-object and a block on REJECT. STE cases: a deliberately failing sentence in why and in how, on a card with intent and on one without, each reported and making the check fail. Mechanical-check cases: positive and negative glued numbers, slash chains and unexplained terms, with task numbers, decision IDs, hashes, versions and repository paths not flagged. More named glossary cases: an alias that appears only inside a longer word is not matched, a zh-TW term absent from the text is not matched, the shorter of two overlapping terms alone is not reported, and empty term, empty text, a non-object locale and a non-list aliases are refused. Change 19, the frozen code root carries the glossary. Why: Change 5 says prompt() reads skills/firstmate/plain-writing.md and i18n/glossary.json from the frozen code root, but snapshot() in bin/fm-herdr.py (around line 595) copies only bin/ and skills/, so a frozen round cannot see i18n/ at all. Round 1 worked around this by reading i18n/ from the live checkout (FM_ROOT) and by treating a missing glossary.json as an empty glossary; both workarounds are removed. How: snapshot() copies i18n/ next to bin/ and skills/ when the source has it, includes its files in the hash inventory and manifest.json, and keeps the same source-changed-during-snapshot check. fm_plain.py reads i18n/glossary.json and i18n/tw2cn.tsv only from the code root it is given; there is no fallback to FM_ROOT or any other checkout. A missing or unreadable glossary.json or tw2cn.tsv is an error everywhere it is read: card checks (fm_ste.py check-plain and fm-decide), pull-request rendering, the advisory lint, zh-CN rendering and spec preflight; each refuses with a message naming the missing file, and none treats it as empty. Test fixtures that copy bin/ into their own code tree and then run a glossary reader from that copy also copy i18n/, the same way they copy bin/ and skills/. Round 1 showed tests/selfupdate.test.sh needs this. The other fixtures that copy bin/ and call fm-decide, fm_ste.py, fm_self_pr.py, fm-review.sh or fm-worker.sh are in scope for the same one-line change, and only where they reach a reader: tests/board-card-effects.test.sh, tests/board-readiness.test.sh, tests/canary.test.sh, tests/decisions.test.sh, tests/review-verdict.test.sh, tests/dispatch.test.sh, tests/reconcile.test.sh, tests/crew-end-to-end.test.sh, tests/setup.test.sh, tests/conventions-publication.test.sh, tests/codex-review-integration.test.sh, tests/board-wake.test.sh, tests/dispatch-owner.test.sh and tests/auth-probe.test.sh. A fixture that never reaches a reader stays unchanged, and no assertion's expected value changes. tests/lib/herdr.py copies i18n/ at both of its stages, the shared class copy (around line 355) and the per-test copy (around line 363), because its workers publish pull requests through the glossary-dependent renderer; its existing assertions stay unchanged. Failure contract and its tests: card checks, pull-request rendering and spec preflight refuse a missing or unreadable glossary.json or tw2cn.tsv with a message naming the file. The advisory lint on posted text (fm_external.py) does not block the post and never uses an empty glossary: it records a lint failure that names the missing file, and the post goes out as today. Tests, in the already scoped files: for each reader boundary (fm_ste.py check-plain, fm-decide, fm_self_pr.py rendering, spec preflight, the posted-text lint), a frozen code root without i18n/glossary.json while FM_ROOT points at a valid checkout that has one, and the same with an unreadable file; each refuses (or, for the lint, records the failure) naming the frozen-root file, proving FM_ROOT is never read. A further case changes the live checkout's glossary after the snapshot and shows the frozen copy still decides. The same cases cover tw2cn.tsv at its readers inside a frozen round: fm_plain.py zh-CN rendering and the zh-CN text that spec preflight puts in the prompt. A missing or unreadable frozen tw2cn.tsv, with a valid conflicting FM_ROOT checkout, is refused naming the frozen file; and after the live table changes, the zh-CN text a frozen round renders still comes from the frozen table. The board (board/server.ts and board/public/index.html) is not a frozen round: it keeps reading i18n/ from the engine checkout it serves, as today, and this change does not touch it. tests/option-loop.test.sh expects fm-review.sh to take 11 value flags (the 9 it has today plus --card and --pr-authoring) and probes both new flags with no value (exit 64). tests/herdr/lifecycle.py asserts that a snapshot of a tree with i18n/glossary.json contains the file and lists it in manifest.json, and that a tree without i18n/ still snapshots. design/design.md section 11 (the paragraph that says the entrypoints freeze bin/ and skills/) names i18n/ as well. Migration: snapshots taken before this change have no i18n/; rounds already running on them use code that predates T-270 and reads no glossary, so they finish as today. The autopilot's reload identity stays bin/ and skills/, so a change to i18n/ alone reaches a running autopilot at its next reload, not at once; this limit is stated in the same design paragraph. Fail-first: on the current base, the lifecycle test that expects i18n/glossary.json in a snapshot fails at its assertion, and the option-loop count assertion fails at 9 versus 11. Overlap: T-271 (PR #259) also edits bin/fm-herdr.py; whichever merges later rebases.
